editorNote: This week catches Atari trying to turn a living-room game machine into a starter computer while IBM PC users keep hearing Lotus 1-2-3 pitched as the new spreadsheet standard.
morningLine: Atari adds a computer keyboard to the VCS conversation, Lotus 1-2-3 keeps pulling office buyers toward the IBM PC, Down Under leads the singles chart, and Tootsie stays atop the weekend box office.

lead.headline: Atari pitches a keyboard path from game console to computer
lead.summary: On February 9, 1983, UPI reported that Atari unveiled a low-cost computer keyboard designed to turn its video-game system into a home computer, a telling sign of how console makers were chasing the family-computing shelf.

computerItems.title: Atari keyboard add-on targets the living room
computerItems.summary: Atari framed the accessory as a way to move beyond cartridges and make a familiar game system feel like a household computer.

computerItems.title: Lotus 1-2-3 is fresh on IBM PC desks
computerItems.summary: Lotus 1-2-3 went on sale in late January 1983, pairing spreadsheet, charting, and database features in one IBM PC package and quickly becoming a business-software talking point.

computerItems.title: Compute! sells an all-new games issue
computerItems.summary: Compute! issue 33, dated February 1983, promoted home, educational, and recreational computing with an all-new games issue and joystick coverage.

computerItems.title: Video-game magazines keep the Atari 5200 and Super Pac-Man in view
computerItems.summary: February 1983 game-magazine shelves highlighted Super Pac-Man, the Atari 5200, and new third-party Intellivision titles as cartridge competition stayed crowded.

briefs.headline: Radio counter: Down Under at No. 1
briefs.summary: The Billboard Hot 100 dated February 12, 1983 put Men at Work's Down Under at the top, with Toto's Africa just behind it.

briefs.headline: Movie counter: Tootsie holds weekend lead
briefs.summary: For February 11-13, 1983, Box Office Mojo lists Tootsie at No. 1, followed by 48 Hrs., The Entity, Gandhi, and Without a Trace.

briefs.headline: Arcade names fill the game aisle
briefs.summary: Super Pac-Man, Zaxxon, Donkey Kong Jr., Pole Position, and Ms. Pac-Man were among the period titles carrying arcade and home-conversion interest into early 1983.

briefs.headline: Home computing sells as family entertainment
briefs.summary: Magazine covers and retail pages kept mixing education, games, joysticks, and BASIC, blurring the line between console play and computer ownership.

market.headline: Console makers chase the computer aisle
market.summary: Atari's keyboard announcement shows how the home-computer boom pressured game companies to promise productivity, programming, and education alongside play.
